# SAT vs ACT: Key Differences and How to Choose in 2026


## TL;DR


The SAT and ACT are both widely accepted college admissions tests, but they differ in format, pacing, scoring, and content. The Digital SAT is shorter and module-adaptive, with Reading and Writing combined with Math on a 400–1600 scale. The Enhanced ACT is linear and includes English, Math, and Reading in its core composite, with Science available as an optional section. The most reliable way to choose is to take a realistic practice test of each, compare your scores using official concordance tables, and then consider your pacing, math, reading, testing format, and college requirements.


---


Both the SAT and the ACT have changed significantly in the last two years. The SAT went fully digital in March 2024. The ACT launched its shorter “Enhanced” format throughout 2025. If you’re reading advice that still mentions a 3-hour ACT or a paper SAT, that information is outdated and could steer you wrong.


This guide covers every meaningful difference between the two tests as they exist right now, gives you the score conversion benchmarks you need, and walks you through a straightforward method for choosing the right one.


[Take a free SAT practice exam](https://miyagilabs.ai/sat/practice-exams) to start figuring out where you stand.

## Key Differences Explained


### Digital SAT vs ACT: Adaptive vs. Linear Testing


One of the most important structural differences between the SAT and ACT is how the tests present questions.


The Digital SAT is **module-level adaptive** . Reading and Writing and Math are each divided into two modules. Your performance on the first module helps determine the difficulty level of the second module.


The ACT is **linear** . Students receive a fixed sequence of questions rather than being routed to a different second module based on earlier performance.


This creates different testing experiences. On the SAT, accuracy early in a section can affect the difficulty of the questions you see later. On the ACT, your test path does not change based on your earlier answers.


For students comparing the tests, the important question is not whether adaptive testing is inherently better or worse. It is whether you perform more consistently when the difficulty of the second module can change based on your first-module performance.


### SAT vs ACT Pacing: Which Test Gives You More Time?


Pacing is one of the clearest practical differences between the SAT and ACT.


The Digital SAT generally gives students more time to work on each question, while the ACT requires faster movement through its sections. This does not mean that the SAT is automatically easier. It means the tests place different demands on time management.

If you tend to spend a long time deciding between two answers, the SAT's pacing may feel more comfortable. If you read quickly and prefer maintaining momentum, the ACT's structure may feel more natural.


The best way to test this difference is to complete a timed practice section from each exam rather than relying on a general description of pacing.


### Reading Style: Short Passages vs. Long Passages


The reading experience feels completely different on each test.


The Digital SAT presents short passages of one to two paragraphs, each paired with exactly one question. You’re constantly shifting between topics, genres, and time periods. It rewards quick comprehension shifts and mental flexibility.


The ACT uses longer passages (roughly 700 to 900 words) followed by multiple questions about the same text. If you prefer sinking into a passage, building a mental model, and answering several questions from that deeper understanding, this approach may feel more natural.


Neither style is inherently easier. They test different cognitive strengths.


### SAT vs ACT Math: Content, Calculator, and Scoring Differences


SAT and ACT Math overlap substantially, but their content distribution and testing experience differ.


The SAT places substantial emphasis on algebra, advanced math, problem-solving, and data analysis. ACT Math covers these areas as well but includes a broader range of geometry and trigonometry.


Another major difference is the calculator experience. The Digital SAT includes a built-in Desmos graphing calculator, while ACT students use an approved calculator under ACT's calculator policy.

### ACT Science vs SAT: What Students Need to Know


The ACT offers a separate Science section, while the SAT does not have a standalone Science test.


Science-related reasoning can still appear on the SAT through questions involving data, evidence, graphs, and scientific contexts. The ACT, however, gives students the option of taking a dedicated Science section.


Because colleges can have different testing and score-reporting policies, students should check the requirements of each school on their college list before deciding whether the optional ACT Science section is useful for their application.


Do not assume that an ACT Science score will automatically provide an admissions advantage. Its relevance depends on the college, program, and testing policy.


If you are considering ACT Science, practice with the current ACT format rather than older four-section ACT materials.


### Scoring: 400-1600 vs. 1-36


The SAT scores on a 400 to 1600 scale, with each section (Reading & Writing, Math) scored from 200 to 800. The Enhanced ACT scores each section from 1 to 36, and the composite is the average of English, Math, and Reading.


There’s no penalty for wrong answers on either test. Always answer every question.


### Paper vs. Digital


The SAT is digital only, taken through College Board’s Bluebook app on a laptop or tablet.


The ACT offers both digital and paper options[as of September 2025](https://enhancedact.org/) . This matters more than people realize. Practitioners on Reddit and test prep forums regularly report that some students perform measurably worse on screens, whether from eye fatigue, difficulty annotating, or simple preference. If screen-based testing is a genuine obstacle for you, the ACT gives you a paper alternative that the SAT simply doesn’t.


## SAT vs ACT for Different Types of Students


The choice between the SAT and ACT can look different depending on your academic strengths and testing preferences.


### SAT vs ACT for Strong Math Students


Students who are particularly comfortable with algebra, functions, and data analysis may want to investigate the SAT because Math represents half of the total SAT score.


However, a strong math background does not automatically make the SAT the better test. Compare actual timed practice scores before deciding.


### SAT vs ACT for Strong Readers


Students who read quickly and are comfortable working through longer passages may find the ACT's Reading section familiar. Students who prefer shorter passages and more narrowly focused questions may prefer the SAT format.


### SAT vs ACT for Students Who Prefer Paper


The SAT is administered digitally, while ACT offers paper testing where available. Students who strongly prefer paper should check the current ACT administration options in their location.


### SAT vs ACT for Students Who Dislike Time Pressure


The SAT generally provides more time per question than the ACT. Students who need additional time to process a question should compare timed practice performance rather than relying only on this general difference.


### SAT vs ACT for STEM-Focused Students


Students interested in STEM should examine the testing requirements of their target colleges and programs. The ACT's optional Science section creates an additional testing component that does not exist on the SAT, but its usefulness depends on the policies of the colleges being considered.


## SAT vs ACT Score Conversion: Concordance Tables


SAT and ACT scores use different scales, so students comparing practice-test results should use an official concordance table rather than comparing the raw numbers directly.


For example, a 1400 SAT and a 30 ACT cannot be compared simply by looking at which number is larger. Concordance tables provide an approximate comparison between the two scoring scales.

## How to Choose: The Diagnostic Method


Forget the question “Is the SAT or ACT easier?” It’s the wrong framing. The right question is: which test matches how you think under pressure? That question has a real answer, and here’s how to find it.


### Step 1: Take a Timed Practice Test of Each


Use the official Bluebook app for the SAT and an official Enhanced ACT practice test for the ACT. Simulate real conditions: timed, no interruptions, no phone.


### Step 2: Convert Both Scores to the Same Scale


Use the concordance table above. If you scored a 1380 on the SAT practice and a 28 on the ACT practice, note that a 28 ACT converts to roughly 1310 on the SAT scale. That’s a 70-point gap favoring the SAT.


### Step 3: If One Score Is Clearly Higher, Choose That Test


A difference of 3 or more ACT points (or 60 or more SAT points) is a strong indicator. At that margin, the higher-scoring test is almost certainly your better option. One test prep consultant put it simply: a 3-point ACT gap “should be considered a pretty firm indicator,” absent significant extenuating factors.


### Step 4: If Scores Are Close, Use Tiebreakers


When your converted scores land within 1-2 ACT points or 40 SAT points of each other, let your strengths decide:


-


**Math is your best subject?** Lean SAT. Math is half your total score.


-


**Fast reader who works quickly?** Lean ACT. The pacing rewards speed.


-


**Prefer paper testing?** ACT is your only option.


-


**Struggle with long reading passages?** Lean SAT. Its short-passage format avoids that challenge.


-


**Applying to STEM programs?** Consider the ACT with optional Science to show that skill.


### Step 5: Check Your College List


Confirm testing policies at your target schools. Six of eight Ivy League schools now require SAT or ACT scores for 2026-2027 admissions. MIT, Caltech, Stanford, Georgetown, and UT Austin also require scores. But over 90% of four-year colleges remain test-optional according to[FairTest data](https://fairtest.org/test-optional-list/) .


Even at test-optional schools, submitting scores is increasingly common. Common Application data shows that roughly 80-85% of applicants to selective test-optional schools now submit SAT or ACT scores, up from about 55-60% during the 2021-2022 cycle. Strong scores help. Weak scores can be withheld. It’s a one-way advantage.


If you want to practice both tests before committing,[try free ACT practice exams](https://miyagilabs.ai/act/exams) alongside the SAT to see where you perform best.


## Do Colleges Prefer the SAT or ACT?


For colleges that accept both tests, students should generally focus on the test that produces the strongest result under the institution's current testing policy.


Colleges set their own admissions testing requirements, recommendations, and score-reporting policies. Some require SAT or ACT scores, some remain test-optional, and policies can change between admission cycles.


This means students should not rely on a general statement such as "colleges prefer the SAT" or "colleges prefer the ACT."


Instead, check each college's official admissions website for:


-


Whether SAT or ACT scores are required


-


Whether testing is optional


-


Whether superscoring is used


-


Whether the college considers all scores or selected scores


-


Whether additional testing requirements apply


-


Which admission cycle the policy applies to


For students applying to multiple colleges, create a simple testing-policy spreadsheet before deciding how much time to invest in SAT or ACT preparation.


## How Many SAT and ACT Practice Tests Should You Take?


You do not need to take dozens of practice tests to decide between the SAT and ACT. Start with one realistic, full-length practice test for each exam.


If the results are clearly different, use the stronger result as one piece of evidence and investigate why the difference occurred.


If the results are close, take another practice test for each exam under comparable conditions.


A useful diagnostic process is:


1.


Take one full-length SAT practice test.


2.


Take one full-length ACT practice test.


3.


Convert the scores using official concordance information.


4.


Identify which sections produced the biggest differences.


5.


Take another practice test for each exam if the results are close.


6.


Choose your preparation path based on the consistent pattern and your college requirements.


The important factor is consistency, not a single unusually high or low practice score.


---


## Do Colleges Prefer One Test Over the Other?


No. Every accredited U.S. college accepts both the SAT and ACT equally. No admissions office penalizes you for submitting one instead of the other.


What has changed is the testing landscape around the test-optional question. After widespread pandemic-era test-optional policies, the pendulum is swinging back. Columbia, the last Ivy League holdout on permanent test-optional admissions, reversed course in June 2026 and will require the SAT or ACT starting with 2027-2028 applicants. Harvard, Yale, Dartmouth, Brown, Cornell, and Penn already require scores for the current cycle.


The practical takeaway: testing matters more in 2026 than it did in 2022. Even if your target school is test-optional, a strong score is an asset worth pursuing.


For context on volume, approximately 1.97 million students took the SAT in 2024 compared to 1.37 million ACT test-takers. The SAT is more popular nationally, but neither test carries more weight in admissions.


---


## The Enhanced ACT: What Changed and Why It Matters


The Enhanced ACT rollout happened in stages. In April 2025, the new format launched for online national Saturday tests. By September 2025, it arrived on the paper national test as well, and the three-section composite calculation became standard for all ACT administrations.


Key changes compared to the old ACT:


-


**44 fewer questions** across the test


-


**Science became optional** and no longer factors into the composite


-


**Math questions dropped from 5 answer choices to 4**


-


**Total core time dropped to 2 hours and 5 minutes**


-


Content and question styles stayed largely the same


One important nuance: fewer questions means each question carries more weight. There’s less room for errors to get averaged out. Students who relied on a high volume of easy questions to offset a few mistakes will find less cushion.


If you’re preparing specifically for this new format, dedicated[ACT prep resources](https://miyagilabs.ai/act/prep) that reflect these changes are essential. Practice materials based on the old 215-question ACT won’t give you an accurate picture.


---


## Superscoring: How It Works for Each Test


Superscoring means a college takes your best section scores across multiple test dates and combines them into a single highest possible composite.


Most colleges that superscore do so for the SAT. You might take the SAT twice and submit your higher Math score from one sitting and your higher Reading & Writing score from another.


ACT superscoring is less universal but growing. The Enhanced ACT’s three-section composite (English, Math, Reading) simplifies the superscoring calculation compared to the old four-section format.


Check each college’s specific policy. Some superscore one test but not the other. Some superscore both. A few accept only single-sitting scores. The College Board and ACT both provide score-sending options that support superscoring. You can read more about[how SAT superscoring works](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/how-to-calculate-your-sat-superscore) for a deeper walkthrough.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### Is the SAT or ACT easier?


Neither is objectively easier. They test overlapping but different skill sets with different structures. The SAT gives more time per question and emphasizes algebra. The ACT moves faster and tests broader content. The “easier” test is whichever one aligns with how you think, which is why taking a practice test of each is the most reliable way to decide.


### Can I take both the SAT and ACT?


Yes. Many students take both, especially early in junior year, to determine which one yields a higher score. You only submit the scores you choose, so there’s no risk in trying both.


### Should I submit both SAT and ACT scores to colleges?


Usually, no. Submit whichever score is stronger when converted via concordance tables. Submitting both doesn’t provide an advantage and can sometimes create confusion if one score is noticeably weaker. Focus your prep energy on one test after your diagnostic comparison.


### Is ACT Science required?


No. As of September 2025, the Science section is optional and does not count toward your composite. The core ACT costs $68; adding Science costs $72. Consider taking it if you’re applying to STEM-focused programs where a strong Science score could serve as a positive signal.


### Does the Digital SAT use the same concordance table as the old paper SAT?


Yes. College Board designed the Digital SAT to maintain score continuity with the previous paper version. A 1400 on the Digital SAT represents the same level of readiness as a 1400 on the old SAT. The 2018 concordance tables remain valid for converting between Digital SAT and ACT scores.


### What is the SAT’s adaptive format, and can it hurt my score?


The Digital SAT’s two-module system routes you to a harder or easier second module based on your Module 1 performance. If you struggle in Module 1, the easier Module 2 caps your maximum possible score for that section. This means early accuracy matters. The ACT has no such mechanism, so every question carries equal weight regardless of where it falls in the test.


### When should I start preparing?


Most students begin serious SAT or ACT prep in the spring of junior year, with a target test date in late junior year or early senior fall. A[structured study plan](https://miyagilabs.ai/blog/sat-study-schedule-guide) spanning 8 to 12 weeks gives enough time to build skills without burning out.
